name: Chlorophyll tablets

lead: Chlorophyll tablets are supplements sold as internal deodorants for breath, body, urine and faecal odour. Users take them hoping to smell fresher from the inside.

They usually contain chlorophyllin, a water-soluble semi-synthetic salt of chlorophyll also used as a food colouring (E140 and E141). Chlorophyllin is claimed to bind odour compounds. A randomised, double-blind crossover study in 28 colostomy patients found no difference from placebo in subjective odour, and Wikipedia calls the deodorant claims unsubstantiated.

paras: People take them as tablets or capsules with food, usually as a daily supplement. Users who try them for odour report on it over a period of days to weeks.
The sources reviewed give no adverse-effect profile. Chlorophyllin is a permitted food colouring.

web.title: Chlorophyll, acne, and TikTok: Should these mix?
TikTok users insist chlorophyll water is healing their acne (dermatologist comments)

angle.text: Chlorophyll tablets are marketed as internal deodorants, and users take them hoping to reduce breath and body odor. In the one controlled odor trial, in 28 colostomy patients, results did not differ from placebo.

lead: Chlorophyll tablets contain chlorophyll or, more often, chlorophyllin, a water-soluble semi-synthetic salt of chlorophyll used as a food colouring (E140 and E141).[1] They are marketed as internal deodorants: people take them in the hope of fresher breath and less body, urine and faecal odour, so that they smell cleaner without applying anything to the skin.[1]

The idea has a long history. Mid-twentieth century marketing put chlorophyllin into toothpaste, soaps and sanitary products, and in the 2020s social-media influencers revived it in the form of 'chlorophyll water'.[1] Wikipedia describes the deodorant claims as unsubstantiated, and the only randomised odour trial found, in 28 colostomy patients, showed no difference from placebo in subjective odour.[1][2]
Research interest in chlorophyllin today is largely in other areas: laboratory studies on its binding of mutagens, and registered trials in radiation-related conditions.[1][3][4][5][6]

Beyond odour, chlorophyll became a skin and acne topic around 2020 to 2021, when videos of people adding liquid chlorophyll drops to water drew hundreds of millions of views, according to a medical-student commentary.[7] Followers of the trend say the green drink gives them clearer skin. Dermatologists quoted in coverage say that studies on chlorophyll and skin have mostly used topical products, sometimes with light therapy, rather than oral drops.[7][8]
infobox: Food colouring and green photoblocker in 3D-printed hydrogels [1]
Breath, body and faecal odour; skin and acne (influencer era)

paras: Wikipedia credits F. Howard Westcott's 1940s research with identifying chlorophyllin as an odour blocker. Companies added it to toothpaste, soaps, and sanitary products in a marketing wave from 1950 to 1953, then dropped it as the hype faded; social-media influencers revived it as chlorophyll water in the 2020s.[1] A 1952 paper examined chlorophyll tablets for faecal odours.[9]

Internal chlorophyllin preparations are marketed to reduce odours from incontinence, colostomies and body odour, and chlorophyllin has also been used as a home acne remedy and as a topical product for wounds and burns, claims that Wikipedia describes as unsubstantiated.[1] On T Nation, members mention sodium copper chlorophyllin as an ingredient in multivitamins and as part of supplement stacks for oestrogen metabolism, and one member describes taking it with large meals after reading about reduced DNA markers of liver damage.[10][11][12]

Chlorophyllin is a group of water-soluble, semi-synthetic salts derived from chlorophyll. The sodium salts are used as food colourings: the magnesium form is E140(ii) and the copper complex is E141(ii).[1] In vitro, chlorophyllin binds environmental mutagens including the polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons benzo[a]pyrene and dibenzo[a,i]pyrene.[1]

In the 2020s, chlorophyll drops stirred into water became a social-media trend among people seeking clearer skin and fewer blemishes. A 2021 commentary by two medical students placed the #chlorophyll hashtag at about 300 million views and grouped it with other viral skin trends.[7] The commentary reviewed what research exists: a randomised controlled trial of topical chlorophyllin for sun-damaged skin (2015), a randomised trial of 24 participants of Asian descent finding chlorophyll-a combined with photodynamic therapy safe for acne, and a report associating oral chlorophyll with improved facial wrinkles. It stated that current research does not show that ingested chlorophyllin improves acne.[7]

Dermatologist Muneeb Shah, who has a large TikTok following, told Yahoo Lifestyle in 2021 that liquid chlorophyll has not been proven to affect acne or redness, pointing to small studies on topical chlorophyllin and suggesting that any improvement could come from drinking more water.[8] Both sources suggest that people who want chlorophyll can obtain it from leafy green vegetables.[7][8]

Common effects listed for chlorophyll supplements include diarrhoea and discoloured urine or stools, and users in forums report green stools after liquid chlorophyllin.[7][13][14] Case reports have linked self-medication with chlorophyll or its derivatives to pseudoporphyria, a rare blistering condition on sun-exposed skin, in people with disturbed porphyrin metabolism.[7] Wikipedia's chlorophyllin article does not cover side effects.[1] Shah likewise described the pseudoporphyria risk from heavy liquid chlorophyll use as low but possible.[8]

Chlorophyllin was a commercial fashion of the early 1950s, when brands added it to toothpaste, sanitary towels and soaps, before use of it in those products faded; the Wikipedia article adds that the underlying research was later considered questionable.[1] The 2020s revival moved the ingredient from deodorant marketing to wellness and skin content, where it is sold as 'chlorophyll water' and drops.[1][7] Chlorophyllin also has a niche use as a photoblocker in 3D printing of hydrogels (2019).[1]

A 1989 randomised double-blind crossover study gave 75 mg chlorophyll tablets three times daily to 28 colostomy patients and found their subjective odour assessments did not differ from placebo.[2] A 1952 report reviewed chlorophyll tablets for faecal odour.[9] Separately, registered trials are testing chlorophyllin for radiation-induced urinary bleeding, oral mucositis, gastrointestinal bleeding and rectal cancer treatment; these do not concern appearance or odour.[3][4][5][6]
Laboratory work shows chlorophyllin binds certain mutagens, and animal and cell studies report other biological effects; Wikipedia describes these as early-stage findings.[1]

Wikipedia reports that chlorophyllin has been described as reducing food-additive-induced genotoxicity, raising expression of the DNA repair proteins p53 and PARP, and modulating cytokine-related proteins such as NFκB and IFNγ, all presented as research findings, not established treatments.[1]

Tablets and chlorophyll drops are discussed as an internal fix for breath and body odour. Forum threads that mention chlorophyllin more often discuss it as a supplement ingredient and report that liquid chlorophyllin turned stools green the next day, which one user said suggested it was passing through the digestive system.[13][14]

lore.intro: Chlorophyll is promoted as an inside-out deodorant, and on T Nation it appears as a supplement ingredient.[13][10]
